title: Target slice and direct algebraic bounds

add.label: Direct inverse
add.name: Inverse theorem
add.statement: Under (I1)–(I6) in the linked inverse conditions, every nonzero v∈F_q^{N+1} with v_0=0 and gp(vᵀ)>θ has a short multiple x with x_0=0.
add.proof:
Write ε=ε_tr and μ=μ_tr. All box coordinates are independent and uniform on {2,…,g+1}. A fiber of a rank-e lattice fixes e coordinates after the others are specified, by an invertible row minor of its basis. Its density is at most g^{−e}.

Trimming. For a lattice Θ of rank 1≤d≤3 with basis B, a centered box coordinate has moment generating function sinh(gt/2)/(g sinh(t/2)) by a geometric sum, with limit 1 at zero. Since sinh(x)/x≥1 and (2j+1)!≥6^jj!, this is at most exp(g²t²/24). Hence the centered image Y=Bᵀr_I−y_Θ satisfies E e^{uᵀY}≤e^{uᵀΣ_Θu/2} by independence. For Z=Σ_Θ^{−1/2}Y and an independent standard Gaussian G in dimension d, integrate e^{√(99/100)GᵀZ} in either order: E e^{99‖Z‖²/200}≤E e^{99‖G‖²/200}=10^d. Markov's inequality and (I2) bound the mass removed by 10^d e^{−99R_tr²/200}≤ε.

Integral facts. For rows J of a largest minor, Cramer's rule makes each entry of B_iB_J^{−1} a ratio of a maximal minor to det B_J, hence at most one in magnitude. Thus restriction to J is injective on the span, and ‖y‖_∞≤‖y_J‖₁ there. For saturated Θ a unimodular extension of B gives an integral left inverse, so Bᵀ is onto the integer codomain. If Δ has rank k and all its k-minors have magnitude <q, some nonzero one survives reduction. In Smith form UΔV=S the k nonzero entries are therefore units mod q. If cᵀΔ≡0, the first k entries of cᵀU^{−1} are multiples of q. Set them to zero and multiply by U. This gives an integral relation reducing to cᵀ.

Prefixes. Put J first for a saturated rank-d Θ. Let B_k be the first k rows, d≤k≤|I|, and write B_k=Y_kC_k with Y_k a basis of the integer points of its span and C_k integral. These prefix lattices have rank d and largest minor J. If h_k,m_k are height and maximum fiber mass, then h_k[Z^d:B_kᵀZ^k]=h(Θ): the index is |det C_k| by transpose surjectivity, and minors scale by that determinant. The first prefix is Z^d, with h_d=1 and m_d=g^{−d}; the last is Θ. Adding a row enlarges the transpose image by a cyclic quotient of order s_k=h_{k+1}/h_k. The new coordinate must lie in one class mod s_k in a fiber, and B_kᵀ and Y_kᵀ have the same fibers by invertibility of C_k. Thus m_{k+1}≤m_k⌈g/s_k⌉/g≤m_k, and s_k≥g fixes the new coordinate.
For s=s_k<g we have m_{k+1}^b h_{k+1}^{b−1}≤m_k^b h_k^{b−1}. For s=1 this is monotonicity. Otherwise ⌈g/s⌉/g≤(1+s/g)/s≤s^{−1+1/b}. The last inequality holds for s≥2^b since 1+s/g≤2, and for 2≤s≤2^b by concavity of s^{1/b}−1−s/2^b and g≥2^b. The concave function is zero at 2^b and positive at 2 by ln(2)/b>2^{1−b} for b≥7 (true at 7, with b/2^{b−1} decreasing).
For rank three, the r ratios above one multiply to h=h(Θ). The upper density factor ∏(1/s_k+1/g) over these ratios exceeds 1/h by at most r(1/2+1/g)^{r−1}/g, by telescoping one factor at a time. If r=0 this error is zero; otherwise the bound is maximal at r=2, since the successive ratio after that is (1+1/r)(1/2+1/g)<1. Therefore m(Θ)≤g^{−3}ξ_tr(1/h+1/g). If m(Θ)≥μ, solving for h gives h≤H_3 by (I2); then m(Θ)h≤Γ_3/g³ by (I4).

Image count. Let Θ of rank d∈{1,2,3} on |I|≤N trim a nonempty box set F on I and a new index i′. Each point of its image Φ(F) under Φ(r)=(Bᵀr_I,r_{i′}) has mass at most m(Θ)/g. We need two cases. In the full-dimensional case the image lies in an index-q coset. Set k=d+1, δ=q, J=∅ and B_2=B, with the empty minor assigned determinant 1. In the other case F^⊥ has rank 1≤d′<d, a largest minor J⊆I and restrictions to I in the span of Θ. For its basis Y, Y_J is invertible, so B_J has rank d′. Extend the saturated integral kernel basis of B_J to a unimodular basis of Z^d, with kernel columns last. This changes B to (B_1,B_2) with (B_2)_J=0 and (B_1)_J invertible. Trimming is invariant under this change; form Φ with the new B. The transpose map (a,t)↦(Ba,t) identifies the image's real normal space with that of F by the restriction hypothesis, so k=dim Φ(F)=d+1−d′. Split a basis V of its saturated normal lattice into the first d′ rows V_1 and remaining k rows V_2. Pulling back integral normals gives (B_1)_JV_1=Y_JC for integral nonsingular C, so |det(B_1)_J|·|det V_1|≥h(F^⊥). Dropping the first d′ image coordinates is injective on differences in ker Vᵀ. The projected differences satisfy V_2ᵀx=0 mod V_1ᵀZ^{d′}, a subgroup of index δ=|det V_1| by transpose surjectivity. Use the identity projection in the full-dimensional case.
In both cases the projected convex hull has dimension k in an index-δ coset, so a simplex of its lattice vertices has volume ≥δ/k!. The lattice point bound gives count ≤k!·vol/δ+k≤(k+1)!·vol/δ. The hull lies in an interval of length ≤g times the projected ellipsoid. For j=k−1, that ellipsoid has volume vol(Ball_j)(gR_tr/√12)^j√det(B_2ᵀB_2) by the singular values of its linear map, with Ball_j the Euclidean unit ball. By Cauchy–Binet and (B_2)_J=0, multiplying the square root by |det(B_1)_J| bounds it by h(Θ)√binom(N,j): each block minor is a maximal minor of B. Using binom(N,j)≤N^j/j!, the resulting bound is
Pr[F]·δ·|det(B_1)_J|≤m(Θ)h(Θ)g^j R_tr^j N^{j/2}(j+2)!vol(Ball_j)/√(12^j j!).
The last factor is 2√3, √2π or 20π/(9√2) for j=1,2,3. By (I3) this gives Pr[F]≤Λ_d g^d h(Θ)m(Θ)/q in the first case and Pr[F]h(F^⊥)≤Λ_{d−d′}g^{d−d′}h(Θ)m(Θ) in the second.

Regularization. Suppose saturated Θ on at most N indices has rank d∈{1,2,3} and m(Θ)≥μ+(3−d)ε. We find a regular saturated extension of rank ≤3 losing at most (3−d)ε. Induct downward from the rank-three prefix bound. For d≤2, choose a largest fiber in each prefix, then trim it by R_{k−1} if such a lattice was constructed, obtaining F_k. Then Pr[F_k]≥m_k−ε≥μ+(2−d)ε. Its normal lattice contains Θ_k. If it is larger, its rank e is in [d+1,3] by saturation and Pr[F_k]>g^{−4}. Its density meets μ+(3−e)ε, so induction constructs the regular extension R_k with m(R_k)≥m_k−(3−d)ε. At the final prefix this proves the result if R_k exists.
Otherwise let j be the last prefix with R_j, or d−1. After j+1 the ratios are <g: a ratio ≥g fixes the new coordinate, whose unit vector would be in the normal lattice Θ_{k+1} and vanish on J. Hence m_k(m_kh_k)^{b−1} is nonincreasing from j+1. To prove regularity of Θ it suffices to bound this product there by μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1}. If j=d−1 this is g^{−db}≤μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1} by (I4). Otherwise F_{j+1} is trimmed by R_j of rank e>d and has normal lattice Θ_{j+1}, largest minor J in the old prefix and restrictions in span(Θ_j)⊆span(R_j). The second image bound and regularity of R_j give Pr[F_{j+1}]h_{j+1}≤Λ_{e−d}Γ_e/g^d. By (I4), m_{j+1}≤A_inv Pr[F_{j+1}], while m_{j+1}≤m_j≤Pr[F_j]+ε≤g^{−d−1}+ε≤μP_d^{b−1}. Multiplying m_{j+1} by the bound for (m_{j+1}h_{j+1})^{b−1} gives the desired product by A_inv Λ_{e−d}Γ_e P_d≤Γ_d.

Short representative. Relabel positive coordinates so the nonzero support is the first m. Adding an independent summand cannot increase the largest atom, by averaging translates. A single nonzero coefficient gives density bound 1/g by conditioning on the other coordinates. Thus each nonempty support prefix has guessing probability in (θ,1/g]. Maintain a regular saturated lattice Θ of rank d∈{1,2,3} containing the prefix residue, with m(Θ)≥gp(v_{[i]}ᵀ)−3ε>μ. Start with Z, whose reduction contains v_{[1]}, of height 1 and density 1/g, regular by Γ_1≥1 from (I4) and μ<1/g. Always h(Θ)≤H_d by regularity for d≤2 and the rank-three bound otherwise.
For an extension choose B with ∏_j‖B_j‖_∞≤a_d h(Θ), where (a_1,a_2,a_3)=(1,2,9). Indeed projection onto J has determinant h(Θ), and Minkowski’s second theorem for the ℓ₁ ball of volume 2^d/d! bounds the product of successive minima by d!h(Θ). Mahler bounds the basis lengths by the first two minima and 3/2 times the third, when present; lifting uses the coordinate bound. Express v_{[i]}≡Bc′, let c=(c′,v_{i+1}) and use the image Φ above. Trim a largest modular fiber cᵀΦ=t, giving F with Pr[F]≥gp(v_{[i+1]}ᵀ)−ε>μ. Its image lies in an index-q coset since v_{i+1}≠0. Full dimension would give Pr[F]≤Λ_dΓ_d/q<μ by (I5) and the first image bound.
The matrix Δ of image differences therefore has rank k≤d. The ellipsoid bounds coordinate j differences by 2R_tr√[(Σ_Θ)_{jj}]≤T_tr‖B_j‖_∞, using Cauchy–Schwarz and the formula for Σ_Θ. The last differences are ≤g−1≤T_tr. All these bounds are ≥1, so each k-minor is bounded by d!T_tr^d∏_j‖B_j‖_∞≤d!a_d H_dT_tr^d<q by (I5). Since cᵀΔ≡0 by the modular fiber, lift c to an integral relation on Δ and pull it back by Φᵀ. This is in F^⊥ and reduces to v_{[i+1]}. The normal rank is positive and at most three by the fiber bound and (I5), and m(F^⊥)≥Pr[F]>θ−ε≥μ+2ε. Its regular extension loses at most 2ε, maintaining the invariant.
At the last prefix write v_{[m]}≡Bz_0≠0. The z reducing into the line of z_0 form a lattice of index q^{d−1}. Its B_J projection has determinant h(Θ)q^{d−1}. Condition (I6), including integrality of h in rank three, gives d!h(Θ)q^{d−1}≤β^d. The ℓ₁ ball of radius β has volume (2β)^d/d!, so Minkowski gives a nonzero lattice point B_Jz, shrinking to equality in the volume threshold if necessary. Then 0<‖Bz‖_∞≤‖B_Jz‖₁≤β<q, so the residue is a nonzero multiple of v_{[m]}. Put zeros in the remaining coordinates including 0 and undo the relabeling.

add.label: Direct classification
add.name: Classification
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack with row space of dimension at most three and no kernel vector has a witness in its row space.
add.proof:
Work over K=F_{q^n}. Let U have an F_q-basis of the row space as columns, d its column count, u_j the transpose of its row j, and h_s=Uᵀσ^s(z). No kernel vector means the entries of h_0 are F_q-independent. For s=a,b,c with a=n/2−1,b=n/2,c=n/2+1, assemble W_s from the U-weight coefficients, V-weight coefficients, and the σ^c conjugate of the U assembly, respectively. These have a unique expression W_s=UM_sUᵀ with M_s symmetric: applying a left inverse of U on both sides gives M_s, and the row and column spaces ensure the reconstruction. The ties imply M_s h_t=M_t h_s. The first d of these h_s are independent: a relation with coefficients λ_j would give the nonzero q-linear polynomial Σ_{j<d} λ_j X^{q^j} vanishing on all entries of h_a, hence on their F_q-span of q^d elements. Frobenius preserves their independence and the polynomial has degree at most q^{d−1}, a contradiction. Thus the h_s span K^d. Thus h_s↦M_s extends linearly, since any relation Σ_s λ_s h_s=0 gives (Σ_s λ_s M_s)h_t=0 for every t. Its trilinear form T(h,u,v)=uᵀM(h)v is symmetric by matrix symmetry and the ties on spanning arguments. The tests give T(h,u_j,u_j−u_0)=0 for every h, by linearity from h_s. Writing M_s for M(h_s), we have M_a=σ^a(M_c) and M_b=σ^b(M_b) by the conjugacy and even-degree V assembly.
If u_0=0, choose d of the u_j as a basis. T vanishes on basis triples with repetitions, so can be nonzero only for d=3, with one independent value t on the triples of distinct indices. In those basis coordinates the off-diagonal evaluations of M_s are t times the three coordinates of h_s. The two conjugacy identities, using σ^a(h_c)=σ^b(h_b)=h_0 and the basis over F_q, imply t h_a=σ^a(t)h_0 and t h_b=σ^b(t)h_0. The spanning condition for three vectors in dimension three rules out both h_a,h_b proportional to h_0. Thus t=0, and T=0 would make the stack zero.
With u_0≠0, complete it to a basis u_0,l_1,…,l_{d−1} from the rows. For each binary tuple δ of length d−1 let p_δ be the dual-coordinate vector taking values 1,δ_1,…,δ_{d−1} on this basis, and write w_δ=Up_δ and z_δ=z(w_δ)≠0. The test relations replace each repeated nonzero index of a basis triple by index 0 until distinct; symmetry then makes each triple's value depend only on its set A of nonzero indices. The cubes (hᵀp_δ)(uᵀp_δ)(vᵀp_δ) have entries ∏_{j∈A}δ_j on these triples. The matrix of these entries, indexing tuples by their support B, is the subset incidence matrix 1_{A⊆B}, triangular with unit diagonal under cardinality order. Hence T is a linear combination of these cubes with coefficients c_δ∈K. Pairs also realize all subsets A since d−1≤2; the same matrix proves independence of the squares p_δp_δᵀ.
It follows that M_s=Σ_δ c_δ σ^s(z_δ)p_δp_δᵀ. Comparing square coefficients in the two conjugacy identities shows c_δ/z_δ fixed by σ^a and σ^b, hence by σ since b−a=1. Write χ_δ=c_δ/z_δ∈F_q. Now take any linear passage test L over F_q. It vanishes on every W_s by vanishing on the stack coefficients. Consequently h_0ᵀQh_s=0, where Q=Σ_δ χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)p_δp_δᵀ is over F_q. Spanning gives h_0ᵀQ=0, and F_q-independence of the entries of h_0 gives Q=0. Independence of the squares gives χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)=0 for each δ. Some χ_δ is nonzero, since otherwise all assemblies and thus the stack vanish. The corresponding w_δ has coordinate 0 equal to 1 and its moment matrix passes every test, hence it is a witness.

add.label: Direct view
add.name: View
add.statement: For a target-group expression D and χ∈F_q, if val(D)=χκ identically at r, the sector stacks are symmetric, pass and satisfy the ties, and each W_c r=u_c; the plain key corner is χ. At such an identity, the coefficient D_{ab} for a second-group coordinate b=(H_{j,1}^{leg})^s vanishes unless a is a first-group F_{i,1}^{k_1}. The distinct monomials s_X υ^{k_c} y_i determine the cell and row. At such an identity, changing r to r′ changes the sector-s contribution by α_s Σ_c γ_c yᵀW_c(r′−r). Thus an identity with zero stacks holds formally and has χ=0. A formal identity forces χ=0; formally equal expressions have equal stacks. If D is not χκ identically at r, its probability of equaling χκ over uniform valid coins is ≤d_f/(q−D)≤ε_f. For two non-formally-equal source-group expressions, the analogous equality probability is ≤ε_f at every r.
add.proof:
On the valid coin grid the denominator-cleared equality is polynomial of degree ≤d_f by the degree premise, and its denominator is nonzero there. Each grid factor has size ≥q−D>d_f, so Schwartz–Zippel proves the probability claim and allows polynomial coefficient comparison in the identity case.
Put a=Ω_{12} and b=Ω_{22}. The first-group F exponents are π_{k_1}y_i and π_{k_1}(a y_i+b A_i). For each leg and j the only second-group poles in b are the two H coordinates, with numerators at the pole −a s_leg(B_j−y_j) and s_leg(B_j−y_j), times α_s. Multiply by b and set b=0 after clearing the other nonzero denominators; these other denominators are independent of a,b and can be canceled from the resulting polynomial identity. The constant first-group residues (all elements except F_{i,2}^{k_1}) are 1, ζτ^k, ζ′τ^k, ζ″y_i and π_{k_1}y_i, and the remaining residues are aπ_{k_1}y_i. Let p stand for a constant residue, indexed by its group element, and F for π_{k_1}y_i indexed by the coordinates F_{i,2}^{k_1}. The coefficients in a of degrees 2 and 1 in the pole identity are respectively
−Σ_{s,leg,j,F} α_s D_{F,H_1} F s_leg(B_j−y_j)
and Σ_{s,leg,j} α_s s_leg(B_j−y_j)(Σ_F D_{F,H_2}F−Σ_p D_{p,H_1}p),
where H_1,H_2 denote the respective coordinates in leg, sector and index j. Both vanish.
Replace y by B(τ)+x and take the coefficient of x_j. The factors after substitution at x=0 are independent for a fixed j: α distinguishes sectors, s_X υ^{k_leg} distinguishes legs without π_{k_1}, and 1, ζ, ζ′, ζ″ distinguish the remaining families without π. The powers of τ are independent and the B_i(τ) are independent since B(d_i)=e_i for i=0,…,N. For terms with π_{k_1}, extract ε-degree zero to get π s_X υ^{2k_1+k_leg}, distinct for cells of each kind, with B_i again independent. Hence the degree-two equation sets all F_{i,2} coefficients against H_1 to zero. The degree-one equation kills H_1 coefficients except F_{i,1}, and matches each of those with its F_{i,2},H_2 coefficient.
Next separate degree in α and the homogeneous class π in π,ζ,ζ′,ζ″ and Ω. The class-π pairs are the matched F,H coordinates, F_1 with search bases or G_2, and matching quotient, remainder and cancellation powers with bases. Summing the matched coordinates cancels Ω by matrix inversion. For sector s divide by α_s. Using the factor formula, the resulting equality is Σ_c γ_c b_c+Φ=χ_s κ, where χ_plain=χ and χ_α=−D_K, and
b_c=yᵀ(W_c r−u_c)+yᵀ(W_c−W_cᵀ)A(τ)+(P_{W_c}+h_c Z_c+Z_0 R_c)(τ).
The quotient h_c and allowed remainder R_c collect coefficients of the chunk powers. Each b_c is free of ε, υ and s_X. Φ comprises mask terms, G_2 pairs and cancellation pairs, all independent of s_E,s_O,s_V. Taking ε-degree zero in each s_X term of the equality separates υ^{k_c}, yielding b_c=0 except b_key=χ_s L_ρ and leaving Φ=0. The cell and row uniqueness in s_X υ^{k_c} y_i follows from the same distinct exponents and independent y_i. Comparing the part linear in y at d_0 (A=0) gives W_c r=u_c; evaluating it at ρ and d_j gives (W_c−W_cᵀ)e_i=0 for every i, so W_c is symmetric. The constant parts are the quotient identities with the appropriate sign choices of h_c and R_c; in the key cell evaluation at ρ gives its corner χ_s. Thus each cell passes by the quotient criterion. Collect ε-degree zero and η-degree one in Φ. For each η_a its coefficient is π yᵀt_a(υ) by the mask identity, plus π times terms divisible by P(υ) from its tie bases. Since Φ=0, cancel π and take each y_i coefficient to see P divides every coordinate of t_a.
Only H_1 coordinates depend on r, through s_leg r_j times α_s, and the pole comparison left only F_1 against them. Therefore changing r gives the stated value difference. If the stacks vanish the identity extends to all r′ and the key corner gives χ=0. If the identity already holds for all r then W_c r=u_c for all r implies W_c=0. Applying that implication to the difference proves stack equality for formally equal expressions. To handle source groups, pair the difference with the other group's generator. It has zero stacks and the same value as the difference. If it were identically zero at any r it would be formally zero, contrary to the premise, so the target probability bound applies.

add.label: Direct ledger
add.name: Generic bound
add.statement: Under (P5), E(2Q+2) ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ for every integer 0 ≤ Q < 2^λ.
add.proof: The u² coefficient of E is θ/2+5ε_f≥0. By (P5), E(2)≤2^{−λ} and E(2^{λ+1})≤1. The line joining these upper bounds is u/2^{λ+1}, so convexity bounds E by that line between the endpoints. Put u=2Q+2.

add.label: Direct gp-rank
add.name: Rank bound
add.statement: For either sampler and every stack W of rank d, gp(W)≤g^{−d}. For every v in its row space, gp(vᵀ)≥gp(W).
add.proof: Stack the rows as M. If its column 0 is nonzero, include that column in a column basis; otherwise omit it. Once the coordinates outside that basis are fixed, the equation Mr=u determines the pivot coordinates uniquely modulo q. If 0 is outside the basis, it need not be conditioned on, since it has zero column. The positive-index pivots each hit their prescribed values with independent probability 1/g or zero, and if 0 is a pivot its conditional probability given all positive indices is at most 1/g. Thus each fiber has probability ≤g^{−d}. Since vᵀr is a linear image of Mr, the largest fiber of Mr maps to one value of vᵀr, giving the other inequality.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct reduction
add.name: Reductions
add.statement: For admissible extraction, moving the independent private draws before B_b's run preserves its output law. Let s_b be B_b's success probability on uniform Module-SIS. In the run with bit b, a good first mark with a kernel vector in its stack row space has probability ≤s_b+2ε_f.
add.proof:
The challenge blocks are uniform independent entries for the programmed seed; all other oracle responses and label injections have their experiment law. Thus the simulated run for b has the real law. The private points are independent and affect no simulated answer, so sampling them before the run preserves their joint law with it.
Fix a run with a good first mark of expression D. At a key mark the target record gives D up to formal equality. At a difference mark the current result record minus the old record gives D up to formal equality, by the record invariant. All earlier target-group results returning an existing record agree formally with it, since no earlier mark occurred; their private values agree. At the mark the difference is formally nonzero, so its denominator-cleared polynomial is nonzero of degree ≤d_f. It vanishes at the independent private test point with probability at most d_f/(q−D)≤ε_f. Otherwise the first disagreement rule selects the required difference. Hence one of the two candidates represents D except with probability ε_f.
Every representative of D is identically χκ at the run's search vector and has the same stacks. Only coefficients against the first coordinates of H can contribute to an r-gradient. The view restriction leaves only first coordinates of F against these. Consequently the sector gradient at its recovery point is α_s Σ_{c,i}γ_c y_i W_{c,i} where W_{c,i} is row i of cell c in that sector, and is zero for a zero stack. For any linear functional φ nonzero on the mark row space, its evaluation on this gradient divided by α_sπ is a polynomial of degree at most n+2. Indeed γ_c/π=s_X υ^{k_c}(1+εω^{2k_1}), and the isolated monomials s_X υ^{k_c}y_i have coefficients φ(W_{c,i}), at least one nonzero. Conditioned on earlier recovery points, choose φ annihilating their span if it is proper. The next gradient lies in that span with probability at most (n+2)/(q−D) by Schwartz–Zippel. The mark rank is at most three, so all three span except with probability ≤3(n+2)/(q−D)≤ε_f using n≤D. If the mark is in the alpha sector, the plain stack and its gradients are zero.
When the mark space has a kernel vector and detection and spanning succeed, the output rule finds one from that space, since the plain space is tested first and is zero for an alpha mark. Heaviness gives a short multiple, and the lifting algorithm finds it. Packing gives an MSIS solution. Any earlier nonfailure output is also a solution, since it comes from lifting a kernel vector, and a returned short multiple packs to a solution. Thus the probability of these good marks exceeds the reduction's success probability by at most the two ε_f failure bounds; its success probability is s_b by the run law.

add.label: Direct extractor
add.name: Extractor
add.statement: Every extractor output is ⊥ or a witness. Under the admissible extraction hypotheses, the probability of a good first mark with no kernel vector in its mark row space and no witness output is at most 2/q.
add.proof:
The test returns only a checked witness. Fix a run with the stated mark, and suppose there is no earlier witness output. At a difference mark the recorded result minus its old record is formally equal to the mark expression, so its tested sketches agree. At a key mark the target record agrees with the mark expression. It cannot be a received target-group element, whose stacks are zero, because the mark is good. Nor can it be a fresh guess, because such a mark has no guess variable. It therefore has the sketches of a result already tested. Thus the tests include the mark-sector sketches whenever no witness was already output.
For its symmetric stack W, the probe map (v_c)_c↦Σ_c W_c v_c surjects onto the row space V, since symmetry identifies the column spans with row spans. The three sketches are independent uniform points of V, independently of the run through the mark. The mark is heavy, hence d=dim V≤3 by (P3) and the rank bound. Then their coordinate matrix in a basis has d independent uniform rows in F_q³. The chance of rank loss is at most Σ_{j=0}^{d−1}q^{j−3}<2/q by testing each row against the span of its predecessors. At full rank the tested span is V. The usable-stack witness result provides a witness in V.
